articles.title: What the spec map is
articles.summary: Every paint file comes with a second picture, the spec map. It tells iRacing how shiny, how metallic and how rough each spot of the car is.
articles.what: The colour file says what colour each spot is. The spec map says what each spot is made of. Four values per pixel carry that: R for metallic, G for roughness, B for clearcoat and A for the lighting mask. The paint can be a perfect red and still look like cheap plastic if the spec map is wrong, and the reverse is just as true. Shokker Paint Booth builds both files for you, one pair per car, at 2048 by 2048 pixels covering the whole car laid flat.
when: You wonder why two paints with the same colour look different on track
You want a chrome, a matte or a candy look and need to know what is really changing
You are about to touch any SPEC slider and want to know what it does
how: Pick a finish for a zone. The finish already carries its own spec values.
Look at the finish card or use the Spec Map Inspector to see its R, G and B numbers.
Move SPEC STRENGTH or the R METAL, G ROUGH and B COAT sliders to push the look.
Render. The paint and the spec map are written together.

controls.label: SPEC STRENGTH
controls.effect: Fades the finish spec toward neutral.

tips: Think in two layers: colour is what you see head on, spec is how light plays across it.
A small spec change often moves the look more than a big colour change.
pitfalls: A spec map is not a second colour image. Do not expect it to show colour on the car.
Strong specs on dark paint can look nearly the same as strong specs on light paint. Metal takes its colour from the paint.

deep.heading: How iRacing reads the two pictures
deep.body: iRacing gets two pictures for your car. The paint picture is the colour you see. The spec picture is four numbers per pixel that tell the lighting engine what the surface is made of: red is metal, green is roughness, blue is the clear layer on top, alpha is a lighting mask. The sim lights every pixel from those four numbers, using its sun, sky and your view angle. That is why the same paint can look like wet enamel, brushed steel or flat vinyl without a single colour changing.

deep.heading: Why paint and spec are never judged apart
deep.body: Metal reflection is tinted by the paint colour, while clear-coat highlights are close to white. So a metal value of 255 on a near-white paint gives silver, the same value on a dark red gives dark tinted metal, and on near-black it can vanish. The spec only decides how much of each effect you get. The colour you painted decides what that effect looks like. Judge the two together, on the car, never one without the other.

deep.heading: What Shokker Paint Booth does for you
deep.body: You never paint these four numbers by hand. Every zone has a base finish that sets a starting metal, roughness and coat, then pattern, overlays and sliders move them. At the very end the app raises any coat value below 16 to 16 and any roughness below 15 to 15 unless the pixel is chrome tier (metal 240 or more), so a render cannot hand iRacing a value that whitewashes. The paint goes out as a 24-bit picture and the spec as a 32-bit picture with alpha, both for the same car.

faq.q: Do I have to understand the spec map to use the app?
faq.a: No. Pick a finish and the app sets all four numbers. Read this when you want to tune a shine, fix a washed-out look or build your own material.

faq.q: Does the spec map change how the car drives?
faq.a: No. Spec only changes how the car looks, never how it handles.

faq.q: What happens if there is no spec file?
faq.a: iRacing falls back to the car's normal material and your colours still show. You just lose your custom shine.

faq.q: Why does iRacing look different from the preview?
faq.a: The preview is a quick design view. iRacing lights the real render with its own sun, shadows and materials, and it reads the spec file separately, so shine only shows in the sim.

mistakes.symptom: The finish looks washed out and white in the sim.
mistakes.cause: A clear-coat value between 1 and 15 reached iRacing. That band is treated as no coat or a legacy value.
mistakes.fix: Re-render from the app instead of editing the file by hand. The app raises every coat value to at least 16.

mistakes.symptom: Silver chrome comes out black or grey.
mistakes.cause: Metal reflection takes the paint colour, and the paint under it was dark or mid grey.
mistakes.fix: Paint the zone near-white, or use a Foundation chrome with Use source paint if you want to keep your colours and accept tinted chrome.

mistakes.symptom: I changed a spec value and nothing happened.
mistakes.cause: The old compiled copy of the spec is still loaded by the sim.
mistakes.fix: Render again, then press Ctrl+R in iRacing. If it still looks old, move the compiled spec copy for that car out of the folder and reload.

protips: The preview shows the same colours as the render but not the same shine, so judge shine on the spec views (R METAL, G ROUGH, B COAT) and in the sim.
A dark paint under high metal is buried: nearly black until the right reflection arrives. Colour first, then metal.

articles.title: R channel: metallic
articles.summary: Red is how metal a spot is. 0 is plain paint, plastic or glass, and 255 is solid mirror metal.
articles.what: Metal reflects light with the colour of the paint under it. Plain paint reflects a white highlight on top of its colour. Turn red up and the surface takes more of the first behaviour: richer colour in the highlights, no flat white sheen. A real chrome needs a very light paint colour under it, because metal shows the paint colour. A dark paint with high metal reads as a deliberate dark mirror.
when: You want to move a finish toward or away from metal
You are choosing between pearl, metallic and chrome
how: Open the zone editor, go to the BASE section and find Spec Sliders.
Move R METAL right to add metal or left to remove it. Each tick is 5.
Check the Spec Map Inspector to see the resulting number.

controls.label: R METAL
controls.effect: Adds or removes metallic on top of the finish.

tips: Rough bands for metal: 0-15 plain paint, 16-63 carbon or subtle flake, 64-127 pearl, 128-175 strong pearl or anodized, 176-239 metallic, 240-255 chrome tier.
Foundation values to remember: Pearl 100, Metallic 200, Chrome 255.
pitfalls: High metal on a dark paint hides the colour. That is by design, but surprises people.
Chrome tier (240-255) is the only band allowed to use roughness below 15.

deep.heading: The six metal bands
deep.body: 0 to 15 is plain non-metal: enamel, lacquer, rubber, glass. 16 to 63 is low metal such as carbon, mineral loading or subtle flake. 64 to 127 is pearl, mica and patina. 128 to 175 is strong pearl or anodized metal. 176 to 239 is true metallic: aluminium, gunmetal, brushed titanium, metallic candy. 240 to 255 is chrome tier, the only band allowed to push roughness below 15. Foundation anchors: Pearl 100, Metallic 200, Candy 200, Satin Chrome 250, Chrome 255.

deep.heading: Metal eats the paint colour
deep.body: As metal goes up, the surface shows less of its own diffuse colour and more of a tinted reflection. Past about 240 almost everything you see is reflection, tinted by the paint colour. That is why silver chrome needs near-white paint and why a fully metallic dark red looks nearly black. Partial-metal finishes such as pearl, metallic and satin chrome keep their colour much better than full chrome.

deep.heading: What moves metal after the base
deep.body: Spec Strength pulls metal toward zero: metal becomes metal times strength, so 50 percent of Chrome is about 128. The R METAL slider adds a value from minus 127 to plus 127 under the zone mask and clips at 0 and 255. Spec patterns add their pattern to metal when the M tick is on. After those, the Material Remap tool squeezes metal into a new low-to-high range and the Material Override tool can set it flat, so those two can overrule the slider.

examples.title: Pearl that shimmers but keeps its colour
examples.goal: Get depth without losing the paint colour.
examples.result: A soft pearl shimmer that sits on your own colours, about a third of full metal.

examples.title: Gunmetal sheen on a dark car
examples.goal: Make a dark car read as metal, not as black paint.
examples.result: Dark paint with a real metallic sparkle in sun. Going all the way to 255 would bury the colour instead.

combos.why: Metal says what it is, roughness says how sharp it reflects. Always set them as a pair.
Shows where every metal and roughness pair lands as a material.
Where the R METAL nudge fits in the order of operations.

faq.q: What is the best metal value for chrome?
faq.a: 255. The Foundation Chrome uses metal 255, roughness 2, coat 16. Anything from 240 up is chrome tier.

faq.q: Why is my metallic car dark?
faq.a: Metal reflection inherits the paint colour. Dark paint plus high metal is buried until light hits it. Lower metal to around 180 to 200, or lighten the paint.

faq.q: Is more metal always shinier?
faq.a: No. Shine is mostly roughness. Metal controls what the reflection is made of. A rough, metallic surface is satin or brushed, not shiny.

faq.q: What metal do pearl and candy use?
faq.a: Pearl is 100. Candy is 200 in the current registry, with a low roughness of 15 so the tinted coat reads deep.

mistakes.symptom: Gloss black turned into dark metal.
mistakes.cause: Metal was raised, by a slider, a metallic overlay or a wrong base.
mistakes.fix: Keep metal at 0 with a wet-look gloss such as Wet Look 0, 15, 16 or Gloss 0, 30, 16.

mistakes.symptom: Coloured chrome looks muddy.
mistakes.cause: A dark, over-saturated paint is under the metal and buries the reflection.
mistakes.fix: Use a bright, controlled colour of the same hue under chrome or candy.

mistakes.symptom: Metal slider seems to stop working.
mistakes.cause: It was already at 0 or 255, where the result is clipped.
mistakes.fix: Move the other way, or change the base so there is room above or below.

protips: Metal bands decide the legal roughness: only metal 240 or more may have roughness under 15. A chrome-tier pixel is the one place a mirror is allowed.
Spec Strength is the quick way to get half-metal: 50 percent strength on Chrome gives about 128, a pearl-level metal, without picking another finish.

articles.title: G channel: roughness
articles.summary: Green is how rough a spot is. 0 is a perfect mirror and 255 is dead flat.
articles.what: Roughness decides how sharp or how smeared a highlight is. Low green gives a tight, bright reflection like wet paint. High green spreads the reflection into a soft glow, which reads as satin, matte or flat. Roughness is the biggest single lever for how a finish feels.
when: You want sharper or softer reflections
You want to go from gloss to satin to matte
how: Open the zone editor, go to the BASE section and find Spec Sliders.
Move G ROUGH left for glossier, right for rougher.
Render and look at the highlights on the car, not on the flat template.

controls.label: G ROUGH
controls.effect: Adds or removes roughness on top of the finish.

tips: Roughness bands: 0-14 mirror (chrome only), 15-29 wet gloss, 30-59 high gloss, 60-99 satin gloss, 100-129 satin or eggshell, 130-159 semi-matte, 160-199 matte, 200-229 flat, 230-255 dead flat.
Foundation values to remember: Gloss 30, Satin Chrome 45, Brushed 75, Matte 200.
pitfalls: Smooth gradients in roughness tend to smear highlights across the car. Steps between a few roughness levels give crisper, more controlled reflections.
Roughness under 15 is floored on anything that is not chrome-tier metal.

deep.heading: Nine roughness bands
deep.body: 0 to 14 razor mirror, reserved for chrome-tier pixels. 15 to 29 wet gloss. 30 to 59 high gloss. 60 to 99 satin gloss. 100 to 129 satin or eggshell. 130 to 159 semi-matte. 160 to 199 matte or blasted. 200 to 229 flat. 230 to 255 dead or porous. Anchors: Wet Look 15, Gloss 30, Semi Gloss 55, Satin 95, Eggshell 140, Matte 200, Primer 215, Flat Black 250.

deep.heading: The floor of 15 and the chrome exception
deep.body: Roughness below 15 is reserved for mirror metal, so every render lifts it to 15 wherever metal is under 240. Chrome-tier pixels, metal 240 or more, keep their low values: Foundation Chrome is roughness 2. Pixels that come from a pattern whose own spec amount is on are exempt from this floor.

deep.heading: Smooth ramps smear, steps travel
deep.body: A continuous high-roughness gradient makes the highlight smear across the panel. Quantised roughness steps make the highlight jump in controlled stages as the camera moves, which is how engineered finishes get a sparkle that travels. Spec Strength pivots roughness around 128: roughness becomes 128 plus (roughness minus 128) times strength, so strength 0 gives a neutral 128.

examples.title: Make a car less shiny without changing colour
examples.goal: Tame a too-glossy zone.
examples.result: Roughness rises by 40 so reflections soften. Either control works; the slider adds, the strength pulls toward 128.

examples.title: Satin from gloss
examples.goal: Move from a wet look to a quiet satin.
examples.result: The same colours with a low sheen that hides small flaws.

combos.why: Roughness and coat together make satin versus matte. Raising roughness alone leaves a glossy halo.
G ROUGH is added after patterns and before remap, and is clipped at 15.
The floor of 15 and the chrome exception in one place.

faq.q: What roughness is a mirror?
faq.a: 0 on paper, but only chrome-tier pixels (metal 240 or more) may go under 15. Foundation Chrome uses 2.

faq.q: Why can I not go below 15 on a gloss car?
faq.a: The app lifts non-chrome roughness to 15 on every render because lower values flare badly in the sim.

faq.q: Which is better for matte, roughness or coat?
faq.a: Both. Matte colour is roughly roughness 200 and coat 160, for example. Do not use alpha to fake matte.

faq.q: Does roughness change the colour?
faq.a: Not directly. It changes how wide and bright the reflection is, which can make a colour look lighter or deeper.

mistakes.symptom: Matte paint still has a glossy halo.
mistakes.cause: Roughness was raised but the clearcoat byte was left at 16, so a sharp coat layer sits over a rough base.
mistakes.fix: Raise coat to around 160 as well, or start from Matte (0, 200, 160).

mistakes.symptom: Highlight smears into one large blur.
mistakes.cause: A smooth roughness gradient across the panel.
mistakes.fix: Use a few distinct roughness steps, or a spec pattern, so the highlight moves in controlled jumps.

mistakes.symptom: Mirror finish looks dull.
mistakes.cause: Roughness above 15 on a metal 255 surface, or coat byte high.
mistakes.fix: Start from Chrome (255, 2, 16) and check the B COAT view is dark green-blue, not bright.

protips: Satin is not one number. Eggshell sits at roughness 140, Satin at 95 and Semi Gloss at 55. Pick the base that matches the look instead of dialling roughness blind.
Wet droplets look: base 0, 22, 16 with rims at roughness 15 and the lens at 35 to 70, in 8 to 24 pixel drops.

articles.title: B channel: clearcoat (it runs backwards)
articles.summary: Blue is the clear layer on top of the paint, and it is backwards. 16 is the strongest, shiniest coat and bigger numbers make it duller.
articles.what: Most people expect a bigger number to mean more clearcoat. In an iRacing spec map the opposite is true. Values 0 to 15 mean no clearcoat. 16 is full clearcoat reflectivity, the wettest look. From 16 up to 255 the coat fades toward nothing. In a normal render Shokker Paint Booth raises every blue value to at least 16, so the coat is never in the 1 to 15 dead band that whitewashes in the iRacing shader. Only a spec you imported yourself, or a pattern whose own spec amount is on, may keep an exact 0.
when: You want a wetter or a drier top layer
A finish looks washed out and you suspect the coat value
how: Open the zone editor, go to the BASE section and find Spec Sliders.
Move B COAT left (a negative number) for a glossier coat, right for a duller one. The number is added straight to the coat value, and 16 is the glossiest.
A coat that is already at 16 cannot get glossier, so only the right side does anything there.

controls.label: B COAT
controls.effect: Added straight to the coat value: left is glossier, right is duller. Cannot go below 16.

tips: Coat bands: 16 maximum, 17-31 very strong, 32-63 strong to medium, 64-127 satin, 128-191 dull, 192-254 almost none, 255 none.
Foundation values to remember: Gloss 16, Candy 16, Brushed 65, Matte 160.
pitfalls: Old notes that call 255 the maximum coat are wrong. 255 is the raw maximum but the coat-effect minimum.
Never author values 1 to 15. Resizing a file can create them by accident, and the app raises them to 16.

deep.heading: The backwards channel in full
deep.body: Blue 16 is the strongest active coat. Values rise toward 255 as the coat fades: 17 to 31 very strong, 32 to 63 strong to medium, 64 to 127 satin, 128 to 191 dull, 192 to 254 almost none, 255 none. Values 0 to 15 are treated by the sim as no coat or a legacy value. 255 is the raw maximum byte but the weakest clearcoat. Old notes that call it maximum are wrong.

deep.heading: The floor of 16 and its two exceptions
deep.body: In a normal render every coat value is raised to at least 16, including matte, so no pixel lands in the 1 to 15 band that whitewashes. The two exceptions are pixels from an imported spec (including the SHOKK DROP authored sets) and pixels where a pattern spec amount is on; those keep their exact values, 0 included. Resizing or smoothing a spec picture can create 1 to 15 values by accident, which is another reason to re-render instead of resizing.

deep.heading: Clearcoat quality and strength
deep.body: The quality control maps straight onto the byte: coat = 16 + (1 minus quality) times 239. Quality 1.0 is coat 16, quality 0.5 is about 135, quality 0 is 255. Spec Strength pulls coat toward 16: coat becomes 16 + (coat minus 16) times strength, so strength 0 gives the full glossy 16. Never blend a coat value from 0 to 16 across an edge; the blend passes through the dead 1 to 15 band. Use a hard edge or blend from 16 upward.

examples.title: Candy depth
examples.goal: A deep wet colour on a metallic body.
examples.result: Maximum coat on a tinted base, which is what makes candy look bottomless.

examples.title: Soft matte without glare
examples.goal: A flat stealth finish that does not shine at an angle.
examples.result: Roughness and coat are both high so no wet halo appears. Pushing coat up further removes the last bit of sheen.

combos.why: The pair that separates satin from matte.
Why the coat floor is 16 and where the exceptions are.
The Spec Sculpt Lab applies the same floor to every file it writes.

faq.q: Is a bigger blue number more clearcoat?
faq.a: No. It is the reverse. 16 is the strongest coat and 255 is none.

faq.q: Why does the app raise my coat 0 to 16?
faq.a: Values 1 to 15 whitewash in the sim and exact 0 means coat disabled, which in normal renders is also raised to 16. Only imported specs and pattern-driven pixels may keep 0.

faq.q: What coat do Foundation finishes use?
faq.a: Gloss and Wet Look 16, Pearl 16, Metallic 16, Chrome 16, Candy 16, Satin Chrome 40, Satin 70, Brushed 65, Matte 160.

faq.q: Can I make blue 255 for a matte look?
faq.a: Only with an imported or authored spec. In normal zones values from 192 to 254 give almost-no coat and are the usual matte territory.

mistakes.symptom: Chrome is dull even on white paint.
mistakes.cause: The coat byte is high, for example 255, which removes the coat reflectivity.
mistakes.fix: Use coat 16 on chrome. Check the B COAT view is dark.

mistakes.symptom: A fade between a clear zone and a bare zone looks whitewashed in the middle.
mistakes.cause: The blend passed through coat 1 to 15.
mistakes.fix: Use a hard edge, or keep both sides at 16 or more.

mistakes.symptom: A slider made the coat go the wrong way.
mistakes.cause: B COAT is added straight to the value, so plus means duller.
mistakes.fix: Move B COAT left for glossier, right for duller. Nothing goes under 16.

protips: Offsetting the coat structure a little from the metal and roughness structure gives a depth cue, because the two highlight lobes peak at different angles.
Satin is only 70 on blue but 95 on green. Many satin looks are about roughness. Coat is what makes the edge of a highlight crisp or soft.

articles.title: A channel: the lighting mask
articles.summary: Alpha switches iRacing lighting on or off for each spot. 255 is normal, 128 is reduced and 0 is lighting killed.
articles.what: Alpha is not transparency of the paint. It controls how much of the sky reflection and sun glint iRacing applies. At 255 the spot behaves normally. At 128 the shine is weaker, which can fake shadow or depth. At 0 there is no lighting response at all, which is useful for fake holes or unlit shapes and risky as a normal material tool.
when: You are making an unlit shape such as a fake hole or a glowing decal
You want to flatten shine over a sponsor area
how: Open MASK > Advanced spec utilities and choose Lighting Mask.
Pick Use Source Alpha, Full Lighting A255, Reduced Lighting A128 or Kill Lighting A0.
Apply it to the zone and render.
tips: Keep normal body paint at 255.
The edge between zones blends alpha as well as colour, so a soft edge gives a soft lighting fade.
pitfalls: Alpha 0 over a big area makes the car look like a flat sticker on track.
Alpha stays at 255 unless you set a lighting mask or override, so do not expect holes you did not make.

deep.heading: What alpha really does
deep.body: Alpha is a lighting and specular mask, not opacity and not a matte switch. 255 means full normal lighting, which is the production default and what every normal zone has. 128 reduces the response and is only meant for specialised fake-depth or shadow tricks. 0 kills lighting and specular response completely, useful for faked vents or unlit holes, but a flat sticker look if overused.

deep.heading: Where alpha comes from in a render
deep.body: The spec starts with alpha 255 everywhere. The only things that change it are the Lighting Mask tool, the Material Override tool (when it sets alpha) and an imported spec map. Soft zone edges also blend alpha across the border, so a soft edge gives a soft lighting fade. The Lighting Mask runs together with the other spec tools after the sliders and before the final coat and roughness floors.

deep.heading: Matte is not alpha
deep.body: A common mistake is lowering alpha to get a matte colour. Matte comes from higher roughness and higher clearcoat bytes (for example 0, 200, 160). Reducing alpha only mutes lighting and makes the area look dead and flat, as if it were printed on.

examples.title: Fake grille holes
examples.goal: Make a printed grille look like dark openings.
examples.result: The grille loses all reflection and reads as a dark gap. Use it on small areas only.

examples.title: Subtle depth in a recessed panel
examples.goal: Reduce highlights in a recess without going fully dark.
examples.result: Lighting response is reduced there, so the panel reads as recessed.

combos.why: The three power tools, with Lighting Mask as the one that touches alpha.
Alpha is the one channel the floors do not touch.

faq.q: Should I touch alpha for a normal car?
faq.a: No. Keep it at 255. The app does that for you.

faq.q: Can alpha make a hole in the car?
faq.a: It can fake one for lighting, but it does not change the car shape or the paint.

faq.q: Why does my matte look flat and dead?
faq.a: If alpha was lowered, the lighting response is gone. Reset to 255 and use roughness and coat for matte.

faq.q: Does soft edge affect alpha?
faq.a: Yes. Soft edges blend alpha as well as colour, so a lighting mask fades softly at its border.

mistakes.symptom: A zone looks like a flat sticker on track.
mistakes.cause: Alpha is at or near 0 over a large area.
mistakes.fix: Set the Lighting Mask back to Full Lighting A255, or Use Source Alpha.

mistakes.symptom: Matte colour is not matte.
mistakes.cause: Reduced alpha was used as the matte control.
mistakes.fix: Raise roughness and coat bytes instead, for example start from Matte.

protips: Use Source Alpha in the Lighting Mask tool keeps whatever alpha the zone already has, so it is the no-change choice.
Set a lighting mask only after you are happy with metal, roughness and coat, because it hides their effect where it applies.

articles.title: Reading a spec picture by colour
articles.summary: If you open a spec map as a normal picture the colours tell you the material. Red is metal, green is roughness and blue is the clear layer, mixed together.
articles.what: The spec map holds R, G and B in one picture, so you can read a material by its colour. A pixel that is red with no green means pure mirror-like metal. A green pixel is a very rough non-metal. White is a rough metal with no coat. Nearly black is smooth plain paint. Blue is the strange one because its meaning is backwards, so a blue-heavy pixel is a dull coat, not a glossy one.
when: You open a spec file in an image viewer and want to make sense of it
You compare two finishes and want to see what differs
how: Open MASK > Advanced spec utilities and choose Material Sampler, which opens the Spec Map Inspector.
Click ALL to see the combined map, or R, G, B and A to see one channel alone.
Use the Sample point to read exact numbers.
tips: Anchors to learn: plain gloss is 0, 30, 16. Chrome is 255, 2, 16. Pure red is uncoated mirror metal. Pure green is maximally rough plain paint. Magenta is mirror metal with the coat suppressed.
Black does not mean empty. It means smooth, non-metal, glossy coat.
pitfalls: A very dark spec map is not a dull car. Glossy plain paint is nearly black in R, low in G and low in B.
Do not read the blue channel like brightness.
aliases: what do the spec colors mean

deep.heading: Why spec pictures use odd colours
deep.body: The spec picture is data, not paint. Red holds metal, green holds roughness, blue holds the clear coat, so every colour is a code. Bright green does not mean glossy, it means very rough and matte. Bright blue means a weak clear coat, not the strongest one. Red alone means metal. Yellow, red plus green, is rough metal. White is rough metal with the coat off, which is not chrome and not gloss.

deep.heading: The neighbourhoods worth memorising
deep.body: A dark green-black such as 0, 30, 16 is the normal gloss neighbourhood. Bright red such as 255, 2, 16 is the chrome neighbourhood. Pure green 0, 255, 0 is dead matte. 255, 255, 0 is chalky or oxidised raw metal. Magenta, 255, 0, 255, is mirror metal with the coat suppressed, an extreme corner used by Fractured night carriers, not ordinary gloss.

deep.heading: A trap in the preview
deep.body: The colour views under the live preview show bytes, not a paint job. A hot-pink spec region is just the way high metal, a high coat byte and low roughness pack into colour. On its own it does nothing; the effect needs spatial pattern, crushed dark paint and lighting around it.

examples.title: Reading a gloss car
examples.goal: Confirm a gloss body is healthy.
examples.result: Metal 0, roughness about 30, coat 16: wet-looking paint with no metal.

examples.title: Reading chrome trim
examples.goal: Confirm chrome parts are set up for a mirror.
examples.result: Metal 255, roughness 2, coat 16: a mirror.

combos.why: Click a spot and read the exact bytes instead of guessing from colour.
Blue is backwards; the most common mis-reading.

faq.q: Why is my gloss car green in the spec view?
faq.a: Dark green-black is the code for normal gloss. The green is the roughness byte, around 30.

faq.q: What colour is chrome in a spec picture?
faq.a: Bright red, because metal is 255 and the green and blue bytes are low.

faq.q: What does white mean?
faq.a: Rough metal with the coat off. It is not chrome.

faq.q: Is the spec picture what iRacing shows?
faq.a: No. iRacing reads the numbers and lights the car with them. The picture is only for you.

mistakes.symptom: I thought bright green meant glossy.
mistakes.cause: Green is roughness, so bright green is very rough.
mistakes.fix: Look for dark green or black for gloss. Use the G ROUGH view to confirm.

mistakes.symptom: I thought bright blue meant maximum coat.
mistakes.cause: Blue is backwards: 16 is the strongest coat and bright blue is a weak coat.
mistakes.fix: The strongest coat is a dark blue channel. Check B COAT.

protips: Switch to the single-channel views (R METAL, G ROUGH, B COAT) when something looks wrong. The mixed colour hides which channel is off.
Use the Channels readout to see exact numbers before changing any slider.

articles.title: The metal and roughness grid
articles.summary: Plot metal across and roughness down and every finish has a home. Chrome sits at high metal and low roughness, matte at low metal and high roughness.
articles.what: Most looks come from just two numbers. Metal says what the surface is. Roughness says how sharp it reflects. The four corners are easy: low metal and low roughness is wet paint, high metal and low roughness is chrome, low metal and high roughness is flat paint, and high metal and high roughness is chalky raw metal. Everything else, pearl, satin chrome, brushed metal, is a point between them. The clear layer then adds or removes gloss on top.
when: You want to place a finish on a map of looks
You are building a custom look and need target numbers
how: Choose the corner closest to the look you want.
Pick a Foundation finish near that corner.
Nudge R METAL and G ROUGH in steps of 5 and compare.

controls.label: R METAL
controls.effect: Moves the finish along the metal axis.

controls.label: G ROUGH
controls.effect: Moves the finish along the roughness axis.

deep.heading: Every finish has a home on the grid
deep.body: Put metal across and roughness down. Low metal with low roughness (0 and 15 to 30) is wet paint and gel coat. Low metal with high roughness (0 and 200 or more) is matte and flat. High metal with low roughness (250 or more and 2 to 15) is chrome. High metal with high roughness (180 and 160) is bead blast and sandblasted metal. The middle band is where brushed, pearl and satin chrome live. The coat then adds the polish on top.

deep.heading: Anchor cards with exact values
deep.body: Liquid glaze 0, 15, 16. Wet look 0, 15, 16. Gloss 0, 30, 16. Semi gloss 0, 55, 40. Satin 0, 95, 70. Eggshell 0, 140, 100. Matte 0, 200, 160. Flat black 0, 250, 255. Pearl 100, 40, 16. Metallic 200, 50, 16. Gunmetal 220, 40, 16. Brushed titanium 180, 70, 16. Antique chrome 220, 18, 50. Dark chrome 250, 15, 40. Chrome 255, 2, 16. Satin chrome 250, 45, 40. Candy 200, 15, 16. Carbon fiber 55, 30, 16.

deep.heading: Live finishes move around their anchor
deep.body: Real finishes are not one point. Chrome is 245 plus 10 times a displacement for metal and 2 plus 8 times it for roughness. Dark chrome is 230 plus 20 times a field. Metallic flake is 168 plus up to 24 from the body and 14 from the polish. Pearl layers sit at metal 90 plus 55 times a layer. Quantised steps are what make highlights jump instead of smearing.

faq.q: Where does satin chrome sit?
faq.a: Near metal 250, roughness 45, coat 40: metal like chrome but with soft reflections.

faq.q: What separates pearl from metallic?
faq.a: Metal. Pearl is about 100, metallic about 200.

faq.q: Where is carbon?
faq.a: Low metal, 55, with a gloss roughness of 30. The weave itself comes from a pattern.

faq.q: Why are there matte metals?

protips: The grid is two-dimensional but a good finish uses a third dimension: variation. Flat points look like paint swatches, varied points look like materials.

articles.title: The three iron rules
articles.summary: Three rules are always enforced so the spec map never breaks in iRacing: coat never below 16, roughness at 15 or more unless chrome, and alpha at full lighting unless you change it.
articles.what: These guard rails run on every render. Rule one: the coat value is raised to at least 16 everywhere, so it never sits in the 1 to 15 band that whitewashes in iRacing. Only imported or pattern-driven specs may keep an exact 0. Rule two: roughness is at least 15 wherever metal is under 240. Only mirror chrome, with metal 240 or more, may go lower. Rule three: alpha starts at 255 everywhere, full lighting, and only a lighting mask, a material override or an imported spec changes it. You never have to apply them yourself, but they explain why a slider seems to stop.
when: A slider will not go further than you expect
You edit a spec outside the app and need the safe limits
how: Stay inside the limits when you hand edit a spec map: blue at 16 or more.
Keep roughness at 15 or more unless metal is 240 or more.
Let the app handle alpha.
tips: The Spec Sculpt Lab always exports iron-safe maps.
pitfalls: A hand-edited blue value of 1 to 15 will look washed out in the sim.
Resizing a spec picture can create forbidden values. Re-render instead of resizing.

deep.heading: The exact rules and the numbers behind them
deep.body: Rule one, coat: every coat value is raised to at least 16 (the app calls this the clearcoat floor). Rule two, roughness: wherever metal is under 240, roughness is raised to at least 15. Metal of 240 or more is chrome tier and may keep roughness down to 0. Rule three, alpha: it starts at 255 everywhere and only a lighting mask, an override or an imported spec changes it. After the rules, values are clipped to 0 to 255 and any invalid number becomes a safe value. These run at the very end of a render, so no slider, overlay or tool can slip past them.

deep.heading: Why each rule exists
deep.body: Coat values 1 to 15 sit in the band the sim reads as no coat or legacy, and they whitewash the paint; resizing or smoothing a spec file creates them by accident, so the app removes the whole band. Roughness under 15 is reserved for mirror metal, so a gloss or satin zone is held at 15 and only a chrome-tier pixel can be a true mirror. Alpha stays at full lighting because it is a mask for the lighting response, not a gloss control; dropping it makes an area look dead.

deep.heading: The two places a value may stay below the floor
deep.body: Pixels from an imported or authored spec (the SHOKK DROP sets) keep their exact coat. Pixels from a pattern whose own spec amount is switched on are also left alone, because the pattern carries its own material. Everything else is lifted. If a design truly needs exact no-coat, check the exported file with the Inspector instead of trusting the preview.

faq.q: Can I turn the iron rules off?
faq.a: No. They protect every file from values that look wrong in the sim.

faq.q: Why is my chrome allowed roughness 2 but my gloss is not?
faq.a: Only pixels with metal of 240 or more may go below 15. Gloss has metal 0, so it is held at 15.

faq.q: Does a hand-edited spec file get checked?
faq.a: Only if you bring it back into the app as an imported spec. Files you edit elsewhere are your responsibility.

faq.q: Does the preview follow the same rules?
faq.a: Yes. The preview runs the same final rules as the export.

mistakes.cause: Normal zones are floored at 16. Only imported specs and pattern-driven pixels keep 0.
mistakes.fix: Use coat 16 for the shiniest look, or import an authored spec if you really need coat off.

mistakes.symptom: A blend between a clear zone and a bare zone looks whitewashed.
mistakes.cause: The blend crossed coat 1 to 15.
mistakes.fix: Hard-edge the zone, or keep both sides at 16 or more.

mistakes.symptom: A roughness below 15 got lifted.
mistakes.cause: The pixel is not chrome tier.
mistakes.fix: Raise metal to 240 or more if you want a mirror there.

protips: The iron rules are a safety net, not a design tool. If a slider hits one, the look is telling you to change the base finish instead.
Resizing a spec picture in an editor can reintroduce illegal values. Re-render at 2048 instead.

articles.title: Paint and spec work together
articles.summary: A finish looks good when the paint and the spec disagree in the right way. Pair a warm matte with a cool metal, and give neighbours contrast.
articles.what: Paint is colour and spec is surface. The finishes that pop most are the ones where they pull against each other. Put a warm, matte area next to a cool, shiny one, and the eye reads two materials even if both are similar in brightness. A spec that is the colour-opposite of the paint also works. And since iRacing shows the car small and moving, one loud hero area plus fine texture beats a dozen competing effects. Keep numbers and sponsors on calm, readable areas.
when: Your car looks flat even though the colours are right
You want to choose finishes for neighbouring zones
how: Choose a hero zone and give it your boldest finish.
Give the neighbouring zones a finish with the opposite character: matte beside gloss, warm beside cool.
Render and judge the car at a distance, not the flat template.
tips: Complementary contrast between neighbouring zones beats raw saturation.
Fine texture of 8 to 32 pixels on the 2048 canvas looks rich at speed. Large blobs look like smeared paint.
pitfalls: A spec that matches the paint character everywhere reads as a plain car.
More effects is not better. One hero area wins.
aliases: why does my car look flat

deep.heading: What actually makes a finish pop
deep.body: Saturation alone does not pop. Complementary neighbour contrast does: deep blue beside warm gold, black beside hot pink, white beside red. Then make the spec the colour-opposite of the paint: a warm paint on matte next to a cool colour on metal reads richer than one shine everywhere. Adjacent areas should differ in colour or in shine, ideally both. One loud hero area (hood or a big panel), calm neighbours, and fine texture for depth, not big blobs.

deep.heading: Paint guidance by material
deep.body: Silver chrome: near-white neutral paint. Coloured chrome or candy: a bright, controlled colour, since an over-saturated dark paint buries the mirror. Pearl: body hue plus lighter and darker flake colours, because a uniform paint makes the spec look pasted on. Gloss black: near-black paint with metal kept at 0. Matte colour: a normal body hue with roughness and coat raised, never reduced alpha. Weathering: oxide colours lined up with the worn spec.

deep.heading: A palette that reads as expensive
deep.body: Two or three colours plus one accent looks expensive; five looks cheap. A good split is about 60 percent dominant, 30 percent accent, 10 percent trim. Candy, pearl, metallic, satin or gloss in the livery colour read premium on big areas; chrome on a large area is loud and shows every flaw, so use it on accents, trim and thin lines. A chrome pinstripe on a matte car reads as real chrome.

faq.q: Why does my bright colour look flat?
faq.a: Probably the shine is the same everywhere. Add a neighbour with the opposite shine.

faq.q: Does more saturation help?
faq.a: No. Contrast between neighbours helps. More saturation mostly muddies a spec.

faq.q: What goes behind numbers?
faq.a: A calm gloss, satin or matte with strong colour contrast. Avoid sparkle, strong patterns and colour-shifting finishes there.

faq.q: Chrome on the whole car?
faq.a: It is loud and shows every flaw. It works as a show-car statement, but accents and trim usually look better.

mistakes.symptom: Everything is metallic and nothing stands out.
mistakes.cause: One shine used all over.

Flat paint with chrome trim lines is the modern retro look; gloss everywhere is the showroom look.

articles.title: How base, pattern and spec combine in a zone
articles.summary: In every zone the base finish gives the starting paint and spec, the pattern adds shape on top, and the spec overlays add surface detail last.
articles.what: Think of a zone as a short stack. First the base finish sets colour and spec. Then a pattern, up to five per zone, is laid over the paint. Pattern spec amount, if set, also carries the pattern into the spec map. Then up to five spec overlays add surface detail only to the spec, with no colour change. Finally the spec sliders, strength and blends tune the end result. Zones with lower numbers win where they overlap.
when: You are not sure which control changes colour and which changes shine
Two settings seem to fight each other
how: Set the base finish and its colour first.
Add a pattern and set its paint mode, opacity and scale.
Add a spec overlay if you want texture without colour.
Finish with SPEC STRENGTH and the R, G and B sliders.

controls.label: SPEC STRENGTH
controls.effect: Fades the base spec toward neutral.

tips: Overlay mode for a pattern hides the base colour with the pattern own colours. Use Blend to keep the paint colour.
Spec overlays never change the colour, so they are the safe way to add texture to a colour you like.
pitfalls: A pattern with spec amount at 0 does not touch the spec map. This is on purpose.
The lower-numbered zone wins an overlap.

deep.heading: Step 1: which zone owns each pixel
deep.body: Every zone builds a mask from its colour match or drawn area, softened with a small blur (about 2 pixels) unless the zone has Hard Edge on, and Hard Edge is on by default in every zone. Zones are processed in list order and an earlier zone claims first: where two overlap, the lower number wins and the later one is cut back. A soft mask above 0.15 is hardened to full ownership. At the end a zone replaces the spec fully where its mask is above 0.5, blends linearly between 0.05 and 0.5, and leaves the spot alone below that. Paint is blended by the mask in the paint stack.

deep.heading: Step 2: the paint stack inside a zone
deep.body: In order: the base finish paint (skipped when the colour mode is Use source paint, so only the spec changes); the base colour mode (solid, gradient, finish colours); hue, saturation and brightness inside the mask (hue up to 180 degrees either way, skipped if all three are under half a percent); base scale placement; then BASE STRENGTH, which mixes the result over your original paint. Patterns come after Base Strength, so lowering it never dims a pattern. Last come the second to fifth base overlays.

deep.heading: Step 3: the spec stack inside a zone
deep.body: In order: the base finish spec; SPEC STRENGTH pulling metal toward 0, roughness toward 128 and coat toward 16; base scale, rotation and clear-coat quality; a second base blended through its gradient; spec patterns (metal, roughness and coat ticks); pattern spec amount; second to fifth base overlays; then the versioned spec overlays, applied last on the finished material as a mix toward their target. After the finish is built: an imported spec map if present, spec placement, then the three SPEC sliders (R, G, B), then Material Remap, Material Override and Lighting Mask, in that order.

deep.heading: Step 4: after every zone is done
deep.body: The app protects numbers and sponsors: wherever the decal mask is on, the original colour is restored so no overlay can repaint them. Wear is applied in one pass, scaled per zone. Decal spec finishes and spec stamps are blended in by their own alpha. Then the final floors run (coat at least 16, roughness at least 15 under metal 240) and the paint and spec files are written. Preview runs exactly the same steps at a smaller size.

faq.q: Does Base Strength change the shine?
faq.a: No. Base Strength only blends the paint toward your original colours. SPEC STRENGTH changes the shine.

faq.q: Which zone wins when two overlap?
faq.a: The one higher in the list (lower number). + Add Zone puts the new zone at the bottom, so it loses overlaps until you drag it up; Chat and presets place new zones at the top.

faq.q: What runs last, my slider or my overlay?
faq.a: The overlays run first as part of the finish, then the R, G and B sliders, then Remap, Override and Lighting Mask.

faq.q: Does the preview match the export?
faq.a: It runs the same steps and floors at a smaller size, so very fine detail can look different from the full render.

mistakes.symptom: My pattern is not dimmed when I lower Base Strength.
mistakes.cause: Patterns are added after Base Strength.
mistakes.fix: Lower the pattern opacity instead.

mistakes.symptom: A zone changes nothing.
mistakes.cause: A higher zone covers it, the colour match selects nothing, or Base Strength or intensity is low.
mistakes.fix: Check the list order, then the zone mask, then the strength sliders.

mistakes.symptom: Sponsors got a chrome look.
mistakes.cause: The body zone also grabbed the sponsor layer, and decals take the material under them.
mistakes.fix: Limit the body zone to the car paint layer and use a decal spec finish for the sponsors.

protips: Quick triage order for any odd look: zone owner, then base colour mode, then Base Strength, then SPEC STRENGTH, then the sliders.
There are at most five pattern layers and five spec overlays per zone, and each zone renders with its own random seed, so two zones with the same finish never repeat exactly.

articles.title: Colour space, files and preview truth
articles.summary: The paint file is an ordinary colour picture and the spec file is raw data. iRacing builds its own version from them, so a stale build can hide your newest file.
articles.what: Shokker Paint Booth writes two files per car: a 24-bit paint TGA and a 32-bit spec TGA with an alpha channel, both 2048 by 2048. The paint is read as normal screen colour. The spec is read as straight numbers, with no colour correction. That is why a pretty spec picture on screen only matters as data. iRacing then compiles the TGAs into a faster .mip file, and an old .mip can show instead of your new TGA until it is rebuilt.
when: Your car looks old in the sim after a fresh export
You open the spec TGA in an image editor
how: Export or deploy the car.
If the sim shows an old look, delete the stale .mip for that car so iRacing rebuilds it.
Never apply colour management or sharpening to a spec file.
tips: Judge finishes on the car preview or in the sim, not on the flat template.
The preview is a close guide, not a perfect copy of the sim shader.
pitfalls: Saving the spec through a photo editor can shift values and break the iron rules.
Wireframe and mask overlays in the preview can hide the real finish. Turn them off before judging.

deep.heading: Two files, two kinds of data
deep.body: The paint file is 24-bit colour, read as normal screen colour. The spec file is 32-bit with alpha and is read as raw numbers, with no colour correction. Both are 2048 by 2048 for a standard car, and the size must match the car template exactly, or iRacing shows the paint shop colours instead. An optional normal map can be written from the metal channel.

deep.heading: The compiled copy trap
deep.body: The first time iRacing loads your files it compiles the spec into a faster copy next to it. If you render again and the look does not change, that compiled copy is stale. Press Ctrl+R in the sim to reload the car textures. If the old shine still shows, move that car's compiled spec copy out of the folder and reload. Other drivers only see your spec if the compiled copy is shared too; Trading Paints shares it.

deep.heading: Byte order and tools
deep.body: The spec file stores its bytes as blue, green, red, alpha, while tools show red, green, blue, alpha. That is normal, so never swap channels by hand. Saving the spec through a photo editor can shift values, apply colour management or sharpen edges, all of which break the iron rules.

faq.q: How big must the paint be?
faq.a: Exactly 2048 by 2048 (or 1024 by 1024), 24-bit.

faq.q: Why do other drivers not see my shine?

faq.q: Why is my paint all black?
faq.a: It was saved with the template alpha channel instead of 24-bit, or 2048 paint textures is off in the sim.

faq.q: Do I need the spec file at all?
faq.a: No. Without it iRacing uses the car normal material. Your colours still show.

articles.title: Spec strength and independent spec
articles.summary: SPEC STRENGTH fades a finish spec toward neutral. INDEPENDENT SPEC lets the spec have its own scale instead of following the base, and SPEC ROTATION turns the spec at any time.
articles.what: SPEC STRENGTH runs from 0 to 100 percent. At 100 you get the finish as designed. Lower it and metal drifts toward 0, roughness toward 128 and coat toward 16, so the look softens without changing colour. INDEPENDENT SPEC (the tick box in the Spec Scale row) unlocks SPEC SCALE so the spec texture can be bigger or smaller than the base. SPEC ROTATION is always available.
when: A finish is too loud and you want it calmer
You want the shine texture to run in a different direction from the paint
how: Open the zone and find SPEC STRENGTH. Drag it in steps of 5.
Tick the INDEPENDENT SPEC box in the Spec Scale row to unlock SPEC SCALE. SPEC ROTATION is always live.
Render and compare.

controls.label: SPEC STRENGTH
controls.effect: Scales metal, roughness and coat toward neutral.

controls.label: INDEPENDENT SPEC
controls.effect: Frees spec scale and rotation from the base.

tips: Behind the slider: metal times strength, roughness moves toward 128 and coat toward 16.
pitfalls: Strength 0 is neutral, not dull: coat goes to 16, the glossiest value.

deep.heading: The exact maths of SPEC STRENGTH
deep.body: Strength pulls the base finish toward a neutral plate: metal becomes metal times strength, roughness becomes 128 plus (roughness minus 128) times strength, coat becomes 16 plus (coat minus 16) times strength. At 100 percent nothing changes. At 50 percent Chrome (255, 2, 16) becomes about (128, 65, 16). At 0 you get metal 0, roughness 128, coat 16, a neutral gloss. It runs on the base spec before patterns and overlays, so those keep their own strength.

deep.heading: Three strengths that are easy to mix up
deep.body: SPEC STRENGTH changes the shine and leaves colour alone. BASE STRENGTH blends the base paint over your original paint and leaves the spec alone. INTENSITY scales how strong a base texture generator is. Use the right one: less shiny means SPEC STRENGTH, more subtle colour means BASE STRENGTH or intensity, smaller pattern means scale, not strength.

deep.heading: Independent spec
deep.body: By default the spec texture follows the base scale and rotation, so a brushed grain turns with the brushed paint. Tick the INDEPENDENT SPEC box in the Spec Scale row to unlock SPEC SCALE so the shine texture can be finer or larger than the paint. SPEC ROTATION turns the spec at any time. Only the spec moves; the colour stays put.

faq.q: Does strength 0 mean dull?
faq.a: No. It is neutral: metal 0, roughness 128, coat 16, a plain gloss. Coat 16 is the glossiest coat.

faq.q: Which slider makes the car less shiny?
faq.a: SPEC STRENGTH, or G ROUGH plus 40.

faq.q: Does strength change colour?
faq.a: No. Only the spec.

faq.q: Why can I not change SPEC SCALE?

mistakes.cause: Strength pulls toward a neutral plate, so every finish converges on plain gloss at 0.
mistakes.fix: Lower in small steps, or change the base finish.

mistakes.symptom: I used strength to shrink a pattern.
mistakes.cause: Strength is not size.
mistakes.fix: Use scale. Smaller number means finer and more repeats.

protips: Authored imports (SHOKK DROP sets) ignore SPEC STRENGTH on purpose, so their hand-tuned numbers stay exact.
The same slider also scales the noise in noisy bases, so on those the effect is a bit stronger than the plain formula.

articles.title: Spec scale and rotation
articles.summary: SPEC SCALE resizes the texture in the spec map and SPEC ROTATION turns it. Both work on the spec only.
articles.what: Where a finish has a texture in its spec, such as brushed grain or a weave, scale makes it bigger or smaller and rotation turns it. Scale runs from 0.05 to 5 times, with 1.00 as the finish default. Rotation goes from 0 to 355 degrees in steps of 5. Because the canvas covers a whole car, a small scale usually looks richer than the default.
when: Brushed grain looks too coarse or runs the wrong way
A weave or flake needs to be finer
how: Tick the INDEPENDENT SPEC box in the Spec Scale row to unlock SPEC SCALE.
Drag SPEC SCALE below 1.00 for finer detail.
Drag SPEC ROTATION to turn the grain.

controls.label: SPEC SCALE
controls.effect: Resizes spec texture.

controls.label: SPEC ROTATION
controls.effect: Turns spec texture.

tips: Features of 8 to 32 pixels read as fine detail on the car.
pitfalls: SPEC SCALE stays locked until INDEPENDENT SPEC is ticked. SPEC ROTATION is always live.
Large scale on a whole car looks like big smears.

deep.heading: What scale really does on a whole car
deep.body: The canvas is 2048 by 2048 and covers the entire car. A feature of 8 to 32 pixels reads as texture; 64 pixels is the size of a side mirror. Scale runs from 0.05 to 5 times with 1.00 as the finish default, and smaller means more repeats, so 0.30 to 0.60 is typical for fine detail. The app also auto-scales a pattern to the zone size: 1.0 if the zone's bounding box covers more than 60 percent of the canvas, otherwise about the square root of that area share, between 0.15 and 1.

deep.heading: Spec placement is its own pass
deep.body: After the zone finish is built, a separate placement pass moves, turns, scales and flips only the spec. That is why independent spec scale and rotation never recolour anything. Rotation goes 0 to 355 degrees in steps of 5.

deep.heading: The fine-detail rule
deep.body: Fine is 4 to 8 pixels, micro is 1 to 2 pixels (car-scale sparkle), and 8 to 32 pixels is the sweet spot for a finish that reads as material. When detail seems enough, make it 25 to 40 percent finer. If a finish does not show up, add more small events and more channel contrast; do not make the marks bigger.
